newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Weaker currencies lead most E.Europe markets low.
newsitem.headline: Weaker currencies lead most E.Europe markets low.

text.p: Most East European stock markets slumped in the week to Thursday, as some extended losses from the previous week, making a token 0.29 percent gain in Ljubljana the highlight of trading.

A weaker local currency lent turbulence to the Czech market and pulled Warsaw lower. The volatile crown in Bratislava drove volume and turnover to year lows and Budapest slipped in the absence of fresh stimulus.
Croatian shares traded mixed and Bucharest posted gains on Thursday reversing the bearish mood of early-week trading.
The Central European Share Index (CESI), which measures price movements in 72 Hungarian, Polish, Czech, Slovak and Slovenian stocks, fell 1.26 percent.
PRAGUE
Czech shares had a turbulent week as the Czech central bank was forced to allow a depreciation of the crown and a reshuffled government announced new austerity measures.

On Tuesday, when the crown depreciated by around 10 percent versus the dollar and mark, the PX50 posted its biggest gain for over three years. But the bull run was short-lived with analysts citing concerns about the economy as a whole.
Despite the gloom, the Czech Statistical Office released figures on Tuesday showing real April industrial sales rising 10.1 percent year-on-year.
But economists were unimpressed, pointing to continued high wage growth as evidence that the central bank was likely to keep interest rates high to combat inflation.
WARSAW

The Warsaw bourse fell this week due to zloty falls triggered by the Czech crown slump and a busy primary market, but analysts expected it to maintain the almost 2.5-month horizontal trend on the longer term.

They said they expected no major selling or buying at the current prices. If the zloty stabilises after a two-percent fall since Thursday last week the bourse might rise moderately in the next sessions, they said.

Analysts said strong gains were unlikely as Poland's largest commercial Bank Handlowy SA share offering worth one billion zlotys and copper giant KGHM's offer, expected in in July, were drawing capital from the bourse.
BUDAPEST
Hungarian shares declined this week after a two percent gain on Monday and after Tuesday's new trading high of 6,012.20 points.
Lack of fresh incentive pulled the indicator down on Tuesday and in the following days to 5,929.15 points on Thursday, still up 55.56 points over last Friday.

Analysts predicted a sideways trend on the short term, with foreign investors wary of the Czech market hit by a run on the crown in past weeks and paying more attention to Poland that was offering fresh investment opportunities.
BRATISLAVA
Political and economic instability worked in tandem to paralyze activity on the Bratislava Stock Exchange this week, highlighted by a year lows in overall volume and turnover in Thursday's session.
The official 16-share SAX index eased 1.77 points from Monday's open to close at 193.75 on Thursday.

Brokers said investors took flight from the market mainly due to a turbulent money market and the volatile Slovak crown, but also because of fallout from plebiscites on NATO membership and direct presidential elections which were declared void.
LJUBLJANA
Slovenian shares rose 0.29 percent this week, as the blue-chip SBI index climbed 3.9 points to 1,322.37. Turnover fell to 225.6 million tolars from 324.9 million.
Traders said future moves on the market would largely depend on the ratification of the EU association accord, signed last June. Parliament is due to vote within the next two weeks.
Traders said the ratification could push higher the blue- chip index by up to 30 percent in up to three months as foreign investors resumed buying and market liquidity increased.
If the ratification fails, shares could fall by up to 30 percent before end-summer, they forecast.
ZAGREB
Croatian stocks ended the week mixed ahead of a public holiday with Zagrebacka Banka forging ahead on stronger volume.

The bank recouped its recent losses to close at 2,100 kuna with 3,875 shares sold. Its GDRs in London also rose strongly after the bank announced it struck a deal with foreign creditors on a loan for minimum 300 million marks.
Traders expected the market to stay weak in little buying interest. They said foreign investors stood back given Western political pressures on Croatia and too expensive stock prices.
BUCHAREST
The Bucharest stock exchange, which performed poorly early in the week, recovered its poise on Thursday as investors looked with renewed interest at lower-priced stocks.
Most average prices drifted higher, volume rose some 574,000 shares to 2.3 million and turnover climbed by around two billion lei to 6.7 billion.
The first tier dominated the market in thinner early-week trading and on Thursday, when it took 82 percent of turnover.
